title: Job 39:19–30
context: The LORD’s speech continues with the war horse and the birds of prey. He asks whether Job gave the horse its might and mane, made it leap like a locust, and filled it with fearless eagerness for battle as the trumpet sounds; then whether the hawk soars and the eagle builds its nest on the cliff by Job’s wisdom or command. The speech closes with the eagle spying out prey and its young feeding where the slain lie, an unsentimental picture of the created order. Throughout, the questions point to strength, instinct, and freedom that God gave and that Job neither created nor controls (compare Psalm 33:17; Proverbs 21:31). Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about God’s wisdom displayed in creation, his care for creatures great and small (compare Psalm 145:9; Matthew 6:26), and the humility that fits a human creature before him.

verses.text: “Have you given the horse might? Have you clothed his neck with a quivering mane?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job gave the horse its might and clothed its neck with a mane. Strength and beauty come from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the giver of every creature’s capacities. Readers in both traditions commonly read the question as directing Job to the Creator’s wisdom.

verses.text: Have you made him to leap as a locust? The glory of his snorting is awesome.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job made the horse leap like a locust, with awesome snorting. Its power is God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the war horse displaying God’s creative power. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s display of creatures Job did not make.

verses.text: He paws in the valley, and rejoices in his strength. He goes out to meet the armed men.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the horse pawing in the valley, rejoicing in its strength, and going out to meet armed men. It delights in what God gave it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see creaturely vigor reflecting the Creator’s glory. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as celebrating God’s handiwork.

verses.text: He mocks at fear, and is not dismayed, neither does he turn back from the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the horse mocking fear and not turning back from the sword. Its courage is part of its created nature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see boldness given by God, not by human training alone. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the speech’s portrait of creation’s power.

verses.text: The quiver rattles against him, the flashing spear and the javelin.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the quiver rattling and the spear and javelin flashing around the horse. It stands firm amid danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the vivid scene of battle as a setting for creaturely courage. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as description within the LORD’s speech.

verses.text: He eats up the ground with fierceness and rage, neither does he stand still at the sound of the trumpet.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the horse eating up the ground with fierceness, unable to stand still at the trumpet. Its eagerness is striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see energy and instinct given by God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing a creature whose nature Job neither made nor controls.

verses.text: As often as the trumpet sounds he snorts, ‘Aha!’ He smells the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the horse snorting at the trumpet and smelling the battle from afar. It is made for such moments by its Creator.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a creature fitted by God for its role. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s wider point about his wisdom in creation.

verses.text: “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk soars, and stretches her wings toward the south?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether the hawk soars and flies south by Job’s wisdom. Its instincts come from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s wisdom guiding creatures in their seasons (compare Jeremiah 8:7). Both traditions commonly read the question as pointing beyond human knowledge.

verses.text: Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up, and makes his nest on high?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether the eagle mounts up and nests on high at Job’s command. It answers to God alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign ordering of creatures’ ways. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as humbling Job before the Creator’s wisdom.

verses.text: On the cliff he dwells and makes his home, on the point of the cliff and the stronghold.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the eagle dwelling on the cliff and the stronghold. God has given it a secure home far above human reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing fitting places for his creatures. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the speech’s display of God’s care.

verses.text: From there he spies out the prey. His eyes see it afar off.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the eagle spying out its prey from far off. Its keen sight is a gift of its Creator, not of human training.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God equipping creatures for life in their world. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as describing creation as God made it.

verses.text: His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the eagle’s young feeding where the slain are. The speech ends with an unsentimental picture of the wild.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a world God governs that includes death as well as life (compare Psalm 104:21). Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as the text gives it.
